stimuli.title: Seven persons in a row, with favourite vegetables
stimuli.content:
Seven persons Bhavik, Dhwani, Garv, Ipsita, Mayank, Sarthak and Tamanna sit in a straight row, all facing north. Each of them likes a different vegetable among Beans, Brinjal, Cabbage, Carrot, Okra, Peas and Spinach. (Facing north, a person's right is towards the east end of the row.)

- Ipsita sits exactly in the middle of the row.
- Dhwani sits second to the right of Ipsita.
- Mayank sits immediately to the right of Dhwani.
- The person who likes Carrot sits immediately to the left of Ipsita, and that person is Bhavik.
- Garv sits at one of the extreme ends of the row.
- Sarthak is not an immediate neighbour of Garv.
- The person who likes Okra sits immediately to the right of Garv.
- Ipsita likes Spinach, and Mayank likes Brinjal.
- The person who likes Beans sits immediately to the left of the person who likes Cabbage.
stimuli.solution:
Step 1: Number the seats 1 to 7 from the left. Ipsita = 4, Dhwani = 6, Mayank = 7.
Step 2: The Carrot-lover sits at seat 3 and is Bhavik.
Step 3: Garv is at an end; seat 7 is Mayank's, so Garv = 1. Seats 2 and 5 remain for Sarthak and Tamanna; Sarthak cannot sit next to Garv, so Sarthak = 5 and Tamanna = 2.
Step 4: Okra is immediately right of Garv: Tamanna. Ipsita Spinach, Mayank Brinjal.
Step 5: Beans, Cabbage and Peas remain for Garv (1), Sarthak (5) and Dhwani (6). Beans is immediately left of Cabbage, so Sarthak Beans, Dhwani Cabbage and Garv Peas.

| Seat | Person | Vegetable |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Garv | Peas |
| 2 | Tamanna | Okra |
| 3 | Bhavik | Carrot |
| 4 | Ipsita | Spinach |
| 5 | Sarthak | Beans |
| 6 | Dhwani | Cabbage |
| 7 | Mayank | Brinjal |

stimuli.title: Six persons in two short facing rows
stimuli.content:
Six persons Kuhu, Lakshay, Nivedita, Pranit, Sanya and Vishal sit in two parallel rows of three seats each. The persons in Row 1 face south and the persons in Row 2 face north, so each person faces exactly one person of the other row. (Facing south, the right is towards the west; facing north, the right is towards the east.)

- Pranit sits in the middle seat of the row that faces south.
- Lakshay faces Pranit.
- Sanya sits immediately to the left of Pranit.
- Vishal sits immediately to the left of Lakshay.
- Nivedita faces Sanya.
stimuli.solution:
Number the seats 1 to 3 from west to east in both rows.
Step 1: Pranit = Row 1 seat 2; Lakshay faces him: Row 2 seat 2.
Step 2: Pranit faces south, so his left is east: Sanya = Row 1 seat 3. Lakshay faces north, so his left is west: Vishal = Row 2 seat 1.
Step 3: Nivedita faces Sanya: Row 2 seat 3. Kuhu takes the last seat, Row 1 seat 1.

| Seat | Row 1 (facing south) | Row 2 (facing north) |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Kuhu | Vishal |
| 2 | Pranit | Lakshay |
| 3 | Sanya | Nivedita |

stimuli.title: Eight persons on ten facing seats, one vacant seat per row
stimuli.content:
Ten seats are arranged in two parallel rows of five, numbered 1 to 5 from west to east in each row. The persons in Row 1 face south and those in Row 2 face north, so seat k of Row 1 faces seat k of Row 2. Eight persons Bhagya, Darshit, Hritik, Jhilmil, Kalindi, Nirmay, Rudra and Tejasvi sit on eight of the seats, and exactly one seat in each row is vacant. (Facing south, the right is west; facing north, the right is east. Vacant seats are counted as seats.)

- Kalindi faces south and sits in the middle seat of her row; Nirmay faces Kalindi.
- Bhagya sits immediately to the left of Kalindi, and the seat facing Bhagya is vacant.
- Darshit sits second to the left of the vacant seat in his row.
- Hritik sits third to the right of Bhagya.
- Rudra sits at an extreme end of a row.
- Jhilmil faces north and faces Rudra.
stimuli.solution:
Step 1: Kalindi = Row 1 seat 3 (facing south, so her right is west and her left east); Nirmay = Row 2 seat 3.
Step 2: Bhagya is immediately to Kalindi's left: Row 1 seat 4, and the seat facing him, Row 2 seat 4, is vacant. Hritik is third to Bhagya's right (west): Row 1 seat 1.
Step 3: Jhilmil is in Row 2 and faces Rudra, so Rudra is in Row 1, at an end: seat 5 (seat 1 is Hritik's). Jhilmil = Row 2 seat 5.
Step 4: Row 2 already has its vacant seat (4), so Tejasvi and Darshit fill Row 2 seats 1 and 2 and Row 1 seat 2 is vacant. Darshit is second to the left of his row's vacant seat: in Row 2 (facing north, left = west) that is seat 2. (In Row 1 the seat second to the left of vacant seat 2 would be Bhagya's seat 4.) So Darshit = Row 2 seat 2 and Tejasvi = Row 2 seat 1.

| Seat | Row 1 (facing south) | Row 2 (facing north) |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Hritik | Tejasvi |
| 2 | vacant | Darshit |
| 3 | Kalindi | Nirmay |
| 4 | Bhagya | vacant |
| 5 | Rudra | Jhilmil |

stimuli.title: Eight persons around a round table
stimuli.content:
Eight persons Aadhya, Bhrigu, Cauvery, Jagrav, Lohith, Mahika, Ranveer and Sukriti sit around a circular table, equally spaced and all facing the centre. (Facing the centre, a person's right is anticlockwise.)

- Mahika sits opposite Aadhya.
- Lohith sits immediately to the right of Aadhya, and Sukriti sits second to the right of Aadhya.
- Bhrigu sits immediately to the left of Mahika.
- Cauvery sits second to the left of Aadhya.
- Jagrav is not an immediate neighbour of Aadhya.
stimuli.solution:
Put Aadhya at seat 0 and number the seats anticlockwise. Mahika = 4. Lohith = 1, Sukriti = 2. Bhrigu (immediately left of Mahika) = 3. Cauvery (second to Aadhya's left) = 6. Seats 5 and 7 remain for Jagrav and Ranveer; seat 7 is next to Aadhya, so Jagrav = 5 and Ranveer = 7.

Anticlockwise from Aadhya (each person's right is the next seat anticlockwise): Aadhya, Lohith, Sukriti, Bhrigu, Mahika, Jagrav, Cauvery, Ranveer

stimuli.title: Ten persons around a round table
stimuli.content:
Ten persons Agastya, Binal, Chanchal, Dhairya, Ipshita, Kanishk, Nandan, Pavani, Shaurya and Vanshika sit around a circular table, equally spaced and all facing the centre. (Facing the centre, a person's right is anticlockwise.)

- Nandan sits opposite Agastya.
- Dhairya sits second to the right of Agastya.
- Only one person sits between Dhairya and Binal when counted to the right of Dhairya, and that person is Shaurya.
- Chanchal sits third to the right of Nandan.
- Vanshika is an immediate neighbour of Nandan.
- Kanishk sits immediately to the left of Chanchal.
- Ipshita sits immediately to the left of Agastya.
stimuli.solution:
Put Agastya at seat 0 and number the seats 0 to 9 anticlockwise. Nandan = 5. Dhairya = 2, Shaurya = 3, Binal = 4. Chanchal = 5 + 3 = 8 and Kanishk = 7. Nandan's neighbours are seats 4 (Binal) and 6, so Vanshika = 6. Ipshita = 9, and Pavani takes the last seat, 1.

Anticlockwise from Agastya: Agastya, Pavani, Dhairya, Shaurya, Binal, Nandan, Vanshika, Kanishk, Chanchal, Ipshita

stimuli.title: Square table: corners facing out, sides facing in
stimuli.content:
Eight persons Avni, Chirantan, Gulabo, Jaiveer, Lavleen, Prithvi, Tanuja and Yashpal sit around a square table. Four of them sit at the four corners and face outside (away from the centre); the other four sit at the middle of the four sides and face the centre. (Facing the centre, the right is anticlockwise; facing outside, the right is clockwise.)

- Avni sits at a corner of the table.
- Prithvi sits immediately to the left of Avni, and Yashpal sits opposite Avni.
- Gulabo sits second to the right of Prithvi.
- Tanuja sits immediately to the left of Gulabo.
- Chirantan sits immediately to the left of Yashpal.
- Jaiveer sits at the middle of a side.
stimuli.solution:
Number the seats 0 to 7 anticlockwise with Avni's corner as 0; corners are the even seats.
Step 1: Avni faces outside, so her left is anticlockwise: Prithvi = 1. Yashpal = 4.
Step 2: Prithvi faces the centre, so his right is anticlockwise: Gulabo = 3. Gulabo faces the centre, so her left is clockwise: Tanuja = 2.
Step 3: Yashpal (corner, facing outside) has his left anticlockwise: Chirantan = 5.
Step 4: Seats 6 (corner) and 7 (side) remain; Jaiveer sits at a side: Jaiveer = 7, Lavleen = 6.

Anticlockwise from Avni: Avni (corner, facing outside), Prithvi (side, facing the centre), Tanuja (corner, facing outside), Gulabo (side, facing the centre), Yashpal (corner, facing outside), Chirantan (side, facing the centre), Lavleen (corner, facing outside), Jaiveer (side, facing the centre)

stimuli.title: Seven persons, one empty chair, facing in or out
stimuli.content:
Eight chairs are placed around a circular table, equally spaced. Seven persons Abhimanyu, Chitrangada, Devraj, Gauhar, Malti, Parikshit and Satyam sit on seven of them; one chair is vacant. Some of the persons face the centre and the others face outside. (Facing the centre, the right is anticlockwise; facing outside, the right is clockwise.) Positions such as 'second to the right' count chairs, including the vacant one.

- Abhimanyu faces the centre, and the vacant chair is second to his right.
- Satyam sits opposite Abhimanyu.
- Devraj sits between the vacant chair and Satyam, next to both.
- Gauhar sits immediately to the left of Satyam, and Parikshit sits immediately to the right of Gauhar.
- Devraj sits second to the left of Malti.
- Parikshit faces the same direction as Abhimanyu, and Chitrangada faces the direction opposite to Parikshit's.
- Exactly three persons face outside.
stimuli.solution:
Put Abhimanyu at chair 0 and number the chairs anticlockwise.
Step 1: Abhimanyu faces the centre, so chair 2 is vacant. Satyam = 4, and Devraj (between the vacant chair and Satyam) = 3.
Step 2: If Satyam faced the centre, his left (clockwise) would be chair 3, Devraj's; so Satyam faces outside and Gauhar = 5. If Gauhar faced outside, his right would be chair 4 (Satyam); so Gauhar faces the centre and Parikshit = 6. Chairs 1 and 7 remain.
Step 3: Devraj is second to Malti's left. From chair 1 facing outside (left = anticlockwise) that is chair 3 — it fits; from chair 7 either way it is chair 1 or chair 5 — neither is Devraj's. So Malti = 1 and faces outside, and Chitrangada = 7.
Step 4: Parikshit faces the centre like Abhimanyu, so Chitrangada faces outside. Outside: Satyam, Malti, Chitrangada — three — so Devraj faces the centre.

Anticlockwise from Abhimanyu: Abhimanyu (facing the centre), Malti (facing outside), vacant chair, Devraj (facing the centre), Satyam (facing outside), Gauhar (facing the centre), Parikshit (facing the centre), Chitrangada (facing outside)

stimuli.title: Six cricketers around a table, with their runs
stimuli.content:
Six persons Hrishikesh, Inder, Jasmit, Kaveri, Lalitesh and Nayantara sit around a circular table, equally spaced and all facing the centre. In a match each of them scored a different number of runs among 12, 18, 25, 31, 40 and 47. (Facing the centre, a person's right is anticlockwise.)

- The person who scored 47 runs sits opposite the person who scored 12 runs.
- Inder scored 31 runs and sits immediately to the left of Kaveri, who scored the fewest runs.
- Hrishikesh sits opposite Inder.
- The runs of Hrishikesh's two immediate neighbours add up to 87.
- Jasmit scored more runs than Nayantara, and Lalitesh scored fewer runs than Hrishikesh.
stimuli.solution:
Put Inder at seat 0 and number the seats anticlockwise.
Step 1: Inder is immediately to Kaveri's left (clockwise of her), so Kaveri = 1, with 12 runs; Inder has 31. Hrishikesh = 3.
Step 2: The 47-scorer sits opposite Kaveri: seat 4.
Step 3: Hrishikesh's neighbours are seats 2 and 4. Seat 4 has 47, so seat 2 has 87 − 47 = 40.
Step 4: Jasmit, Lalitesh and Nayantara take seats 2, 4 and 5. Lalitesh scored fewer than Hrishikesh, and Hrishikesh cannot have 40 or 47 (they are at seats 2 and 4), so Lalitesh cannot hold 40 or 47 either: Lalitesh = seat 5. Jasmit > Nayantara gives Jasmit 47 (seat 4) and Nayantara 40 (seat 2). Hrishikesh and Lalitesh share 18 and 25; Lalitesh has fewer: Lalitesh 18, Hrishikesh 25.

| Seat | Person | Runs |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | Inder | 31 |
| 1 | Kaveri | 12 |
| 2 | Nayantara | 40 |
| 3 | Hrishikesh | 25 |
| 4 | Jasmit | 47 |
| 5 | Lalitesh | 18 |

stimuli.title: Six floors and six favourite sweets
stimuli.content:
Six persons Ayush, Charulata, Dakshesh, Hemangi, Kiranmayi and Sohil live on the six floors of a building, one on each floor. Floor 1 is the lowermost and floor 6 the topmost. Each of them likes a different sweet among Barfi, Halwa, Jalebi, Laddoo, Peda and Rasgulla.

- Ayush lives on floor 3 and likes Halwa.
- Only one person lives between Ayush and Dakshesh, and Dakshesh lives above Ayush.
- Charulata lives immediately above Dakshesh and likes Laddoo.
- Kiranmayi lives immediately above Ayush.
- Hemangi lives on an even-numbered floor.
- The person who likes Peda lives on the lowermost floor, and the person who likes Jalebi lives immediately below Ayush.
- The person who likes Rasgulla lives immediately above the person who likes Barfi.
stimuli.solution:
Step 1: Ayush = 3, Dakshesh = 5, Charulata = 6, Kiranmayi = 4.
Step 2: Floors 1 and 2 remain; Hemangi is on an even floor: Hemangi = 2, Sohil = 1.
Step 3: Peda is on floor 1 (Sohil); Jalebi on floor 2 (Hemangi). Barfi and Rasgulla remain for floors 4 and 5; Rasgulla is above Barfi: Kiranmayi Barfi, Dakshesh Rasgulla.

| Floor | Person | Sweet |
|---|---|---|
| 6 | Charulata | Laddoo |
| 5 | Dakshesh | Rasgulla |
| 4 | Kiranmayi | Barfi |
| 3 | Ayush | Halwa |
| 2 | Hemangi | Jalebi |
| 1 | Sohil | Peda |

stimuli.title: Seven floors and seven monthly rents
stimuli.content:
Seven persons Anvay, Brijesh, Dhruvika, Gunjita, Jasraj, Moksha and Neelesh live on the seven floors of a building, one on each floor (floor 1 is the lowermost, floor 7 the topmost). Each pays a different monthly rent among ₹8,000, ₹9,000, ₹11,000, ₹12,000, ₹14,000, ₹15,000 and ₹17,000.

- Moksha lives on floor 4 and pays ₹14,000.
- The person who pays the highest rent lives two floors below Moksha.
- Jasraj lives immediately above Moksha and pays the lowest rent.
- Anvay lives immediately below Moksha, and his rent is ₹1,000 more than Jasraj's.
- Dhruvika lives on the topmost floor, and the rents of Dhruvika and Gunjita add up to ₹23,000.
- Brijesh pays ₹1,000 more than Moksha, and Gunjita lives below Brijesh.
- Gunjita pays more than Dhruvika.
stimuli.solution:
Step 1: Moksha = 4 (₹14,000). Jasraj = 5 (₹8,000, the lowest). Anvay = 3 (₹9,000). The ₹17,000 payer is on floor 2. Dhruvika = 7.
Step 2: Brijesh pays ₹15,000, so he is not on floor 2. Floors 1, 2 and 6 remain for Brijesh, Gunjita and Neelesh; Gunjita lives below Brijesh, so Brijesh cannot be on floor 1 — Brijesh = 6.
Step 3: Rents left: ₹11,000, ₹12,000 and ₹17,000 for Dhruvika, Gunjita and Neelesh. Dhruvika + Gunjita = ₹23,000 = 11 + 12, so Neelesh pays ₹17,000 and lives on floor 2; Gunjita = 1. Gunjita pays more than Dhruvika: Gunjita ₹12,000, Dhruvika ₹11,000.

| Floor | Person | Rent |
|---|---|---|
| 7 | Dhruvika | ₹11,000 |
| 6 | Brijesh | ₹15,000 |
| 5 | Jasraj | ₹8,000 |
| 4 | Moksha | ₹14,000 |
| 3 | Anvay | ₹9,000 |
| 2 | Neelesh | ₹17,000 |
| 1 | Gunjita | ₹12,000 |

stimuli.title: Nine floors numbered from the top, two vacant
stimuli.content:
A building has nine floors. The floors are numbered from the top: floor 1 is the topmost floor and floor 9 the lowermost. Seven persons Amarjeet, Bhuvanesh, Chinmayee, Durgesh, Pankti, Ritwik and Shalaka live in it, one person per floor, so two floors are vacant. Each person has a different profession among Actor, Baker, Coach, Dentist, Jeweller, Nurse and Plumber.

- Durgesh lives on floor 5 and is a Plumber.
- The Baker lives immediately above Durgesh, and the floor immediately below Durgesh is vacant.
- Bhuvanesh lives on the lowermost floor, and Chinmayee lives immediately above him.
- Pankti is a Dentist and lives immediately above Chinmayee.
- Amarjeet lives three floors above Pankti.
- Exactly one floor lies between Ritwik and Shalaka, and Ritwik lives above Shalaka.
- The Nurse lives immediately above the Baker.
- Ritwik is neither the Actor nor the Jeweller, and the Jeweller lives below the Actor.
stimuli.solution:
Remember: a smaller floor number is higher up.
Step 1: Durgesh = 5 (Plumber); floor 6 is vacant; the Baker is on floor 4.
Step 2: Bhuvanesh = 9, Chinmayee = 8, Pankti = 7 (Dentist). Amarjeet = 7 − 3 = 4, so Amarjeet is the Baker.
Step 3: Floors 1, 2 and 3 remain for Ritwik and Shalaka, with one floor between them and Ritwik higher: Ritwik = 1, Shalaka = 3, floor 2 vacant.
Step 4: The Nurse is immediately above the Baker (floor 4): Shalaka. Actor, Coach and Jeweller remain for Ritwik, Chinmayee and Bhuvanesh; Ritwik is the Coach. The Jeweller is below the Actor: Bhuvanesh (9) Jeweller, Chinmayee (8) Actor.

| Floor (from top) | Person | Profession |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Ritwik | Coach |
| 2 | vacant | — |
| 3 | Shalaka | Nurse |
| 4 | Amarjeet | Baker |
| 5 | Durgesh | Plumber |
| 6 | vacant | — |
| 7 | Pankti | Dentist |
| 8 | Chinmayee | Actor |
| 9 | Bhuvanesh | Jeweller |

stimuli.title: Seven boxes in one stack
stimuli.content:
Seven boxes B, E, G, J, N, S and W are kept one above another in a single stack. Position 1 is the bottom and position 7 the top.

- Box W is kept exactly in the middle of the stack.
- Only two boxes are kept between box W and box G, and box G is above box W.
- Box B is kept immediately above box W.
- Box J is kept at the bottom of the stack.
- Box E is kept immediately above box S.
stimuli.solution:
W = 4, G = 7, B = 5, J = 1. Positions 2, 3 and 6 remain for E, N and S. E is immediately above S, so they take 2 and 3 (S = 2, E = 3), and N = 6.

Bottom to top: J, S, E, W, B, N, G

stimuli.title: Ten boxes in two side-by-side stacks
stimuli.content:
Ten boxes B, D, F, H, K, M, P, R, T and W are kept in two stacks, Left and Right, standing side by side, with five boxes in each stack. Level 1 is the bottom of a stack and level 5 its top. A box is 'directly to the right' of another when it is at the same level of the Right stack.

- Box T is at level 3 of the left stack, and box F is directly to the right of box T (at the same level of the other stack).
- Box P is kept immediately above box F, and box H is at the top of the stack that contains box P.
- Box B is at the same level as box P, in the other stack.
- Box K is at the bottom of the stack that does not contain box H.
- Boxes B and D are in the same stack, and as many boxes are kept above box B as below box D.
- Box W is kept immediately above box M, and box R is not in the stack that contains box W.
stimuli.solution:
Step 1: T = Left 3, F = Right 3, P = Right 4, H = Right 5. B is at level 4 of the Left stack.
Step 2: K is at the bottom of the stack without H: Left 1.
Step 3: D is in B's stack (Left). One box is above B (level 5), so one box is below D: D = Left 2.
Step 4: Left 5, Right 1 and Right 2 remain for M, R and W. W is immediately above M, so they take Right 1 and Right 2 (M = Right 1, W = Right 2); R is in the other stack: Left 5.

| Level | Left stack | Right stack |
|---|---|---|
| 5 | R | H |
| 4 | B | P |
| 3 | T | F |
| 2 | D | W |
| 1 | K | M |

stimuli.title: Eight boxes in eight colours
stimuli.content:
Eight boxes C, E, H, L, O, S, V and Y are kept one above another in a single stack (position 1 is the bottom and 8 the top). Each box is of a different colour among Brown, Cream, Golden, Grey, Navy, Olive, Peach and Silver.

- Box C is kept fourth from the bottom.
- Only two boxes are kept between box C and the Cream box, and the Cream box is above C.
- Box L is kept immediately above box V, which is not Grey.
- Box S is at the bottom and is Navy.
- The Olive box is kept immediately above the Golden box, and box Y is Golden.
- Box O is kept immediately above box C, and box E is kept immediately below box V.
- Box L is Brown, box H is Peach, and box O is not Grey.
stimuli.solution:
Step 1: C = 4; the Cream box is at 7; O = 5; S = 1 (Navy).
Step 2: L is immediately above V and E immediately below V, so E, V, L occupy three consecutive positions among the free ones (2, 3, 6, 7, 8): only 6, 7, 8 work. E = 6, V = 7 (Cream), L = 8 (Brown).
Step 3: H and Y take 2 and 3. The Olive box is immediately above the Golden box Y. If Y were at 2, position 3 would be Olive, but H at 3 is Peach; so Y = 3 and H = 2, and C (position 4) is Olive.
Step 4: Grey and Silver remain for O and E; O is not Grey, so O is Silver and E is Grey.

| Position | Box | Colour |
|---|---|---|
| 8 | L | Brown |
| 7 | V | Cream |
| 6 | E | Grey |
| 5 | O | Silver |
| 4 | C | Olive |
| 3 | Y | Golden |
| 2 | H | Peach |
| 1 | S | Navy |

stimuli.title: Six meetings in six months, with cities
stimuli.content:
Six persons Aruna, Bhaskar, Gauravi, Jitesh, Madhulika and Sameer each attend one meeting in the same non-leap year. The meetings are held in six different months — February, March, May, July, August and November — and in six different cities among Ajmer, Bareilly, Hubli, Jorhat, Nashik and Rourkela. 'Between' and 'next' refer to the order of these six meetings.

- Gauravi's meeting is in a month that has 31 days, and it is held in Jorhat.
- Exactly two of the meetings are held between Gauravi's and Jitesh's, and Jitesh's is earlier.
- Madhulika's meeting is the last of the six.
- Bhaskar's meeting is the next one after Gauravi's, and it is held in Rourkela.
- Aruna's meeting is earlier than Sameer's.
- The Hubli meeting is in the shortest of the six months, and the Ajmer meeting is the one just before Gauravi's.
- The Nashik meeting is in a month that has 31 days.
stimuli.solution:
Step 1: Gauravi's month has 31 days: March, May, July or August. Jitesh is three meetings earlier, so Gauravi is in July (Jitesh February) or August (Jitesh March).
Step 2: Bhaskar is the next meeting after Gauravi's. If Gauravi were in August, Bhaskar would be in November, which is Madhulika's. So Gauravi = July, Jitesh = February, Bhaskar = August.
Step 3: Aruna and Sameer take March and May; Aruna is earlier: Aruna March, Sameer May.
Step 4: Hubli is in February (Jitesh); Ajmer is just before July: May (Sameer). Bareilly and Nashik remain for March and November; Nashik is in a 31-day month: Aruna Nashik, Madhulika Bareilly.

| Month | Person | City |
|---|---|---|
| February | Jitesh | Hubli |
| March | Aruna | Nashik |
| May | Sameer | Ajmer |
| July | Gauravi | Jorhat |
| August | Bhaskar | Rourkela |
| November | Madhulika | Bareilly |

stimuli.title: Appointments on the Tuesdays and Fridays of October 2026
stimuli.content:
A bank's loan officer meets customers only on Tuesdays and Fridays. Eight customers Chandrima, Dheeraj, Farhana, Jugnu, Kshitij, Mahua, Prachi and Rishabh each have one appointment with her in October 2026, on eight different dates; one of the possible dates has no appointment. 1 October 2026 is a Thursday.

- Chandrima's appointment is on the third Friday of the month.
- Only two persons have appointments between Chandrima's and Dheeraj's, and Dheeraj's is later.
- Mahua's appointment is on the last of the nine possible dates.
- No appointment is fixed on the second Friday of the month.
- Farhana's appointment is on the possible date immediately before Chandrima's.
- Kshitij's appointment is on the first Tuesday, and Prachi's is earlier than Kshitij's.
- Jugnu's appointment is on a Tuesday.
stimuli.solution:
Step 1: 1 October is a Thursday, so the Fridays are 2, 9, 16, 23, 30 and the Tuesdays 6, 13, 20, 27: nine possible dates.
Step 2: Chandrima = 16 (third Friday); the 9th has no appointment; Mahua = 30; Farhana = 13 (the possible date just before the 16th). Kshitij = 6 (first Tuesday), so Prachi = 2.
Step 3: The 20th, 23rd and 27th remain for Dheeraj, Jugnu and Rishabh. Two persons sit between Chandrima and Dheeraj, so Dheeraj = 27. Jugnu is on a Tuesday: 20; Rishabh = 23.

| Date | Day | Customer |
|---|---|---|
| 2 Oct | Friday | Prachi |
| 6 Oct | Tuesday | Kshitij |
| 9 Oct | Friday | — |
| 13 Oct | Tuesday | Farhana |
| 16 Oct | Friday | Chandrima |
| 20 Oct | Tuesday | Jugnu |
| 23 Oct | Friday | Rishabh |
| 27 Oct | Tuesday | Dheeraj |
| 30 Oct | Friday | Mahua |

stimuli.title: Five calculus-style inequality symbols
stimuli.content:
In the questions of this set, the symbols ∂, ∇, ∫, ∑ and ∏ are used with these meanings:
'A ∂ B' means 'A is greater than B'; 'A ∇ B' means 'A is smaller than B'; 'A ∫ B' means 'A is equal to B'; 'A ∑ B' means 'A is either greater than or equal to B'; 'A ∏ B' means 'A is either smaller than or equal to B'.
Assuming the statements to be true, find which of the conclusions I and II is/are definitely true.
stimuli.solution: Decode: ∂ means >, ∇ means <, ∫ means =, ∑ means ≥ and ∏ means ≤. Rewrite every statement with the ordinary signs, join them into one chain, and test each conclusion along the chain.

stimuli.title: Coded directions between six points
stimuli.solution:
Put L at (0, 0), with east and north positive.
K α L: K = (6, 0). M β K: M = (6, 8). N γ M: N = (0, 8). O δ L: O = (0, −8). T γ O: T = (−6, −8).

stimuli.title: Three coded sentences about a river
stimuli.content:
In a certain code language:
'river flows fast' is written as 'mo ki ra',
'fast boats sail' is written as 'ki pu zo', and
'boats cross river' is written as 'zo ra te'.
(The codes of the words in a sentence may be in any order.)
stimuli.solution: Each shared word takes the code its two sentences share: river = ra (sentences 1 and 3), fast = ki (1 and 2), boats = zo (2 and 3). The leftover code in each sentence belongs to its only unshared word: flows = mo, sail = pu, cross = te.

stimuli.title: Letter codes with three conditions
stimuli.content:
Each letter is coded as shown below, subject to the conditions that follow.

| Letter | A | B | C | D | E | H | K | M | N | O | R | S | T | U |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| C | o | d | e |
| 4 |
| % |
| 7 |
| @ |
| 9 |
| # |
| 2 |
| $ |
| 5 |
| 8 |
| & |
| 3 |
| © |
| 6 |

Conditions:
(i) If the first letter is a vowel and the last letter is a consonant, the codes of the first and the last letters are interchanged.
(ii) If both the first and the last letters are vowels, both are coded as the code of the second letter.
(iii) If the first letter is a consonant and the last letter is a vowel, the last letter is coded as ★.
If no condition applies, every letter is coded as in the table.
stimuli.solution: Check the first and last letters of the word, apply at most one condition, and code the remaining letters from the table.

stimuli.title: Four coded sentences about plants
stimuli.content:
In a certain code language:
'save water daily' is written as 'ka lo mi',
'water the plants daily' is written as 'mi ne lo su',
'plants need sunlight' is written as 'su ra tu', and
'need to save' is written as 'ra ka vo'.
(The codes of the words in a sentence may be in any order.)
stimuli.solution: plants = su (sentences 2 and 3); need = ra (3 and 4); save = ka (1 and 4). Then sunlight = tu and to = vo. 'water' and 'daily' always appear together, so they share 'lo' and 'mi' in some order; the remaining code of sentence 2, ne, is 'the'.

stimuli.title: Six three-digit numbers
stimuli.content:
Study the following six three-digit numbers and answer the questions.

517   284   936   461   708   359
stimuli.solution: Read each operation carefully and apply it to every number.

stimuli.title: Three rows of numbers with operation rules
stimuli.content:
Each row below has three numbers. Work from left to right: apply the rule that fits the first two numbers, then apply the rule that fits that result and the third number. The final value is the row's result.

(i) If an odd number is followed by an even number, they are added.
(ii) If an even number is followed by an odd number, the odd number is subtracted from the even number.
(iii) If an odd number is followed by an odd number, they are multiplied.
(iv) If an even number is followed by an even number, the first is divided by the second.

Row 1: 15   8   3
Row 2: 36   4   7
Row 3: 28   5   6
stimuli.solution:
Row 1: 15 (odd), 8 (even) → 23; 23, 3 (both odd) → 69.
Row 2: 36, 4 (both even) → 9; 9, 7 (both odd) → 63.
Row 3: 28 (even), 5 (odd) → 23; 23 (odd), 6 (even) → 29.

stimuli.title: Machine: smallest number to the right end
stimuli.content:
A number arrangement machine rearranges a line of numbers step by step. In each step it takes the smallest number among those not yet arranged and places it at the right end, immediately to the left of the numbers already arranged there (in Step I, at the extreme right). The other numbers keep their order. The machine stops when all the numbers are arranged.

Input: 48 13 76 54 29 37 91

stimuli.title: Machine: words rotated and moved to the right
stimuli.content:
A word arrangement machine rearranges a line of words step by step. In each step it takes, among the words not yet arranged, the word that comes first in alphabetical order, moves its first letter to the end of the word (for example, 'pear' becomes 'earp'), and places the new word at the right end, immediately to the left of the words already arranged there. The other words keep their order. The machine stops when every word has been arranged.

Input: plum grape kiwi apple mango lime
stimuli.solution:
Alphabetical order of the input words: apple, grape, kiwi, lime, mango, plum.

Step I: plum grape kiwi mango lime pplea
Step II: plum kiwi mango lime rapeg pplea
Step III: plum mango lime iwik rapeg pplea
Step IV: plum mango imel iwik rapeg pplea
Step V: plum angom imel iwik rapeg pplea
Step VI: lump angom imel iwik rapeg pplea

stimuli.title: Machine: digit products and reversed words
stimuli.content:
A word and number arrangement machine rearranges a line step by step. In each step it makes two moves: (1) among the numbers not yet arranged, it takes the one whose two digits have the smallest product, replaces it by the sum of its digits and places the result at the left end, immediately to the right of the results already placed there; (2) among the words not yet arranged, it takes the one that comes last in alphabetical order, writes it backwards and places it at the right end, immediately to the left of the words already placed there. All other elements keep their order. The machine stops when every element has been arranged.

Input: comet 47 orbit 82 nova 36 lunar 91 star 55
stimuli.solution:
Digit products: 47 → 28, 82 → 16, 36 → 18, 91 → 9, 55 → 25, so the numbers are taken in the order 91, 82, 36, 55, 47 and become 10, 10, 9, 10, 11. Words from last to first alphabetically: star, orbit, nova, lunar, comet.

Step I: 10 comet 47 orbit 82 nova 36 lunar 55 rats
Step II: 10 10 comet 47 nova 36 lunar 55 tibro rats
Step III: 10 10 9 comet 47 lunar 55 avon tibro rats
Step IV: 10 10 9 10 comet 47 ranul avon tibro rats
Step V: 10 10 9 10 11 temoc ranul avon tibro rats

stimuli.title: The lunch-box relay
stimuli.content:
Every working day in some large Indian cities, thousands of home-cooked lunches travel from kitchens in the suburbs to offices in the business district, and the empty boxes return home the same evening. The service is run not by a technology company but by a network of carriers, most of whom have little formal schooling. Yet the boxes almost never go missing.

The secret lies in a simple system. Each box is marked with a short code of letters, numbers and colours painted on its lid. The code shows the station where the box is collected, the station where it is to be delivered, and the building and floor of the office. Carriers do not need to read addresses; they need only to recognise the marks. At every major station, boxes are sorted by code and handed from one team to the next, much like a baton in a relay race.

Timing is just as important as sorting. The carriers depend on local trains, which run to a fixed timetable, and each team knows exactly which train it must catch. A delay of even a few minutes at one point can upset the whole chain, so carriers take great pride in being punctual. Many of them work in the same area for years and come to know their customers by sight.

The system has drawn visitors from business schools and large companies, who come to study how such reliability is achieved without computers. What they often find is that the strength of the network lies less in its tools than in its people: a shared sense of duty, clear roles and a habit of helping a team-mate who falls behind.

The service has had to adapt in recent years. Some customers now book through mobile apps, and food-delivery companies offer competition. Even so, many families still prefer to send food from their own kitchens, and the painted code on the lid continues to do its quiet work.

stimuli.title: The sleepy classroom
stimuli.content:
Teachers of early-morning classes know the scene well: rows of students yawning, heads resting on hands, eyes struggling to stay open. It is tempting to blame late-night phone use, and screens certainly play a part. But sleep scientists point to a deeper cause. During the teenage years, the body clock shifts, so that adolescents naturally begin to feel sleepy later at night than younger children or adults do. A fifteen-year-old who is sent to bed at nine may simply lie awake.

This shift would matter little if teenagers could also wake later. Instead, many schools begin their day early, and long journeys mean that some students leave home before sunrise. The result is a steady loss of sleep through the week, which students try to recover by sleeping late on Saturdays and Sundays. Researchers call this pattern 'social jet lag', because the body is pushed back and forth as if it were crossing time zones every weekend.

The costs go beyond yawning. Students who sleep too little find it harder to concentrate and to remember what they have learnt, and they are more likely to feel irritable or low. Tired teenagers are also more prone to accidents, especially on two-wheelers.

A few schools in different countries have experimented with starting classes later in the morning, often by thirty to sixty minutes. Studies of such schools have generally found that students sleep longer, attend more regularly and arrive less tired, though the effect on examination results varies. The change is not easy to make: bus routes must be rearranged, parents' working hours must be considered, and sports and other activities may be pushed into the evening.

Sleep experts do not claim that a later bell will solve every problem. Their point is narrower but important. A sleepy teenager is not necessarily lazy; he or she may be fighting biology. Schools that take this into account may find that the same lessons, taught an hour later, are better received.

stimuli.title: The magic of ninety-nine
stimuli.content:
Walk into almost any shop and you will see prices such as ₹199, ₹499 or ₹9,999. Few sellers choose these numbers by accident. A price that ends just below a round figure is known as a 'charm price', and retailers have used it for more than a century in the belief that it makes goods seem cheaper than they are.

The belief is not entirely mistaken. Researchers who have studied shoppers' behaviour suggest that people tend to read a price from left to right and give most weight to the first digit. A price of ₹499 is therefore registered as 'four hundred and something' rather than as almost five hundred. The saving of a single rupee is trivial, but the impression of a lower price category can be strong, especially when a shopper is in a hurry or comparing many items at once.

Charm prices also carry a message. Shoppers have learnt to associate them with discounts and bargains, so a price ending in 99 can signal value even when no discount is being offered. For the same reason, sellers of luxury goods often avoid them. A jeweller or a high-end restaurant is more likely to quote a round ₹5,000, which suggests quality and confidence rather than a hunt for bargains.

The effect has limits. When buyers think carefully, as they do before purchasing a house or a car, the pull of the first digit weakens. Some studies have found little or no effect for certain products, and the results vary from one market to another. In addition, as digital payments replace cash, the practical nuisance of receiving small change has disappeared, which may alter how shoppers respond to odd prices.

Still, the persistence of the ninety-nine suggests that sellers find it useful. It is a reminder that a price is not just a number but a piece of communication, and that buyers, however rational they believe themselves to be, read more into it than arithmetic alone would justify.

stimuli.title: A garden plant gone wild
stimuli.content:
In the nineteenth century, a flowering shrub from Central and South America was brought to India as an ornamental plant for gardens. Its small, bright flowers made it popular, and it was later planted along fences and railway lines as a hedge. Today that shrub, lantana, covers vast areas of Indian forests, and ecologists count it among the most troublesome invasive plants in the country.

Lantana spreads with remarkable ease. Birds eat its berries and scatter the seeds widely, and the plant grows quickly in open, disturbed ground, such as the edges of roads or patches cleared by fire. Once established, it forms dense thickets that shade out the grasses and young trees beneath. Because most animals avoid eating its leaves, which are toxic to livestock, there is little to keep it in check.

The consequences reach well beyond the plants it smothers. Grazing animals such as deer find less to eat where lantana dominates, and the predators that depend on them may follow them elsewhere. Villagers who once collected fodder, fuel and medicinal herbs from the forest floor find these resources harder to reach. The thickets can also feed forest fires, since the dry stems burn readily.

Removing lantana has proved difficult. Cutting it back without digging out the roots often leads to vigorous regrowth, and cleared ground is quickly reinvaded unless native grasses are planted at once. Some forest departments have therefore adopted a method in which each plant is uprooted at the base and the area is restored with local species, but the work is slow and labour-intensive.

A few communities have found an unexpected use for the plant. Its tough, flexible stems can be woven into furniture and baskets, and craftspeople trained in this work earn an income while helping to clear the forest. Such efforts cannot remove lantana on their own, given the scale of the problem, but they turn a burden into a modest resource and give local people a reason to keep up the fight.

stimuli.title: Money already spent
stimuli.content:
Suppose you have paid in advance for a concert ticket, and on the evening of the show you feel unwell and the rain is pouring down. Many people would go anyway, reasoning that they cannot let the money go to waste. Yet the money is gone whether they go or not. The only question that remains is whether the evening will be better spent at the concert or at home. Economists call money that has already been spent and cannot be recovered a 'sunk cost', and they argue that it should play no part in decisions about the future.

The advice is simple to state and remarkably hard to follow. People dislike admitting that an earlier choice was a mistake, and abandoning a project can feel like confirming that the resources put into it were wasted. So they continue, sometimes adding more money in the hope of rescuing what has already been spent. Psychologists have found this tendency in individuals, in companies and in governments, and it tends to grow stronger when the person who made the original decision is also the one deciding whether to continue.

Large organisations offer the most expensive examples. A half-built project may consume further funds for years because stopping it would mean writing off the amount already invested and accepting blame for the original plan. Officials may describe the extra spending as 'protecting the investment', a phrase that quietly shifts attention from future returns to past costs.

Not every decision to persist is irrational, however. Sometimes the money already spent has bought something of real value, such as a nearly finished building, a skilled team or knowledge gained through trial and error, that makes completing the project cheaper than starting something new. In such cases, continuing is justified not by the past spending itself but by what it has produced. The difficulty lies in telling the two situations apart honestly.

Some institutions try to do this by separating roles: the people who review a troubled project are not the ones who proposed it. Others set conditions in advance, agreeing at the outset on the point at which a venture will be abandoned. Neither method is foolproof, but both rest on the same insight: the past should inform our judgement of the future, not hold it hostage.

stimuli.title: The pull of the crowd
stimuli.content:
A telephone is useless to the first person who owns one; its value comes entirely from the number of other people one can call. Economists call this a 'network effect': a product or service becomes more valuable to each user as more people use it. Messaging apps, online marketplaces and even languages share this property, and it shapes competition in ways that ordinary products do not.

When network effects are strong, early leads tend to grow. A marketplace with many sellers attracts more buyers, whose presence draws still more sellers. A rival with a better design may struggle to break in, because a customer who switches gives up access to everyone who stays behind. Markets of this kind often tip towards one or two dominant firms, not necessarily because those firms offer the best product but because they reached a large size first.

For users, the outcome is mixed. A single dominant network is convenient: everyone can reach everyone else, and there is no need to juggle several accounts. But a firm that knows its customers cannot easily leave has less reason to keep prices low or to listen to complaints. It may raise the fees it charges to sellers, change its rules without warning or neglect the privacy of its users, confident that few will walk away.

Regulators have experimented with several responses. One is to require 'interoperability', so that the users of one service can communicate or trade with the users of another, much as subscribers of different mobile operators can call one another. Another is to let users carry their data, such as contacts or ratings, when they move to a competitor, which lowers the cost of switching. A third is to build a shared platform on which many firms compete, so that the network itself belongs to no single company.

None of these remedies is free of difficulty. Interoperability can be technically complex and may weaken security if it is designed carelessly, and forcing a network open may reduce the reward for building one in the first place. The challenge is to keep the benefits of a large network, which are real, while preventing its owner from turning those benefits into a toll that users have no choice but to pay.

stimuli.title: Keepers of the light
stimuli.content:
For centuries, lighthouses have warned ships away from rocks and shallow water. Before modern navigation equipment, a sailor approaching the coast at night (1) ______ on these lights to know where he was. Each lighthouse flashes in its own pattern, so that an experienced crew can tell one from another.

Running a lighthouse was once a demanding job. Keepers lived at the station with their families, often on a lonely headland or a small island. They climbed the tower every evening to light the lamp, cleaned the glass so that the beam would not be (2) ______, and kept watch through the night. In stormy weather, they could not leave their post even for a short while.

Over the last few decades, most lighthouses have been (3) ______. Electric lamps now switch on by themselves at dusk, and faults are reported to a distant control room. Satellite navigation has also made the lights far less (4) ______ than they once were. As a result, the old job of the keeper has almost disappeared.

The towers themselves, however, have found new life. Several have been opened to visitors, who climb the narrow stairs to enjoy the view and learn about the history of the coast. Small museums explain how the great lenses work and how the keepers lived. For many coastal towns, the lighthouse has become a (5) ______ that draws tourists and their money.

Sailors still value the lights, too. Electronic systems can fail, and a captain who sees a familiar beam in the darkness knows at once whether his instruments are telling him the (6) ______.

stimuli.title: Mushrooms from straw
stimuli.content:
Every year, after the paddy harvest, farmers in parts of northern India are left with mountains of straw. With little time before the next crop must be sown, many set the fields on fire, sending thick smoke across the region. The practice is (1) ______ by law in many places, yet it continues because the alternatives seem costly or slow.

One alternative turns the problem into a (2) ______. Paddy straw, when chopped, soaked and packed into beds, makes an excellent base for growing certain varieties of mushroom. A small shed, some plastic sheeting and a few weeks of care are enough to produce a crop that can be sold in nearby towns. The leftover material, rich in organic matter, can then be (3) ______ to the fields as manure, improving the soil that produced the straw in the first place.

The idea is not new, but it has spread slowly. Mushrooms are delicate and spoil within days, so growers need quick access to buyers. Many farmers also lack the knowledge needed to keep the beds free of disease. Where cooperatives have stepped in to provide (4) ______ and to collect the produce, the results have been encouraging, and some women's groups now earn a steady income from their mushroom sheds.

Mushroom growing cannot, of course, use all the straw that a region produces. It is one of several (5) ______, along with machines that mix the straw into the soil and plants that turn it into fuel. Together, such measures can reduce burning, but only if farmers find them practical and (6) ______. A ban that offers no workable alternative is likely to be ignored, however strictly it is worded.

stimuli.title: Gold in the vault
stimuli.content:
Long after the world abandoned the gold standard, central banks continue to hold large stocks of gold. To some observers this seems **(1) reasonable**: gold pays no interest, costs money to store and guard, and its price can swing sharply from one year to the next. Why should a modern central bank keep so much of its reserves in a metal that earns nothing?

Part of the answer lies in trust. Unlike a government bond, gold is not anyone's promise to pay, so it cannot be **(2) defaulted** on, and if it is stored at home it cannot be frozen by a foreign government. In times of crisis, when confidence in currencies and financial institutions weakens, gold has tended to hold its value or even rise, which makes it a **(3) risky** hedge against turmoil.

Gold also helps central banks **(4) concentrate** their reserves. A reserve portfolio made up mainly of assets in a single foreign currency leaves a country exposed to that currency's ups and downs; adding gold spreads the risk. In recent years, several central banks in emerging economies have been **(5) reducing** their gold holdings steadily, partly for this reason and partly to lessen their dependence on any one country's financial system.

The case is not without critics. They point out that the price of gold is driven largely by sentiment, and that money tied up in the metal could instead earn interest in bonds. Holding some gold, they concede, may be prudent, but holding a great deal of it amounts to **(6) costly** insurance whose benefits are hard to measure.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What will come in place of the question mark (?)?
? × 6 − 384 ÷ 16 = 13 × 9 + 3

solution.concept: Simplify each side with ÷ and × before + and −, then isolate the unknown
solution.why_others_wrong: 16 subtracts the 24 from 120 instead of adding it; 20 ignores the 384 ÷ 16 term; 144 stops before dividing by 6.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What will come in place of the question mark (?)?
∛? ÷ √0.36 = 15

solution.concept: Evaluate the known root, undo the division, then cube
solution.why_others_wrong: 9 is ∛?, not ?; 3,375 = 15³ forgets the √0.36; 216 = 6³ takes √0.36 as 0.4.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Which of the following fractions lies between 3/7 and 4/9?

solution.concept: Compare by decimals or cross-multiplication; the mediant (a + c)/(b + d) always lies between a/b and c/d
solution.shortcut: Mediant: (3 + 4)/(7 + 9) = 7/16 lies between 3/7 and 4/9.
solution.why_others_wrong: 5/11 and 9/20 are slightly larger than 4/9; 2/5 is smaller than 3/7.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: If 5ˣ = 3, what is the value of 25^(x + 1)?

solution.why_others_wrong: 75 takes 25ˣ as 3 instead of 3²; 34 adds 25 and 9 instead of multiplying; 45 multiplies 9 by 5 instead of 25.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What is the least number that must be subtracted from 6,412 to make it a perfect square?

solution.concept: Find the largest perfect square not exceeding the number
solution.explanation: 80² = 6,400 and 81² = 6,561, so the largest perfect square below 6,412 is 6,400. Subtract 6,412 − 6,400 = 12.
solution.why_others_wrong: 149 must be added to reach 81² = 6,561; 171 goes one square too far down, to 79² = 6,241; 80 is the square root of 6,400, not the number to subtract.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What will come in place of the question mark (?)?
0.125 × 0.64 ÷ 0.016 + 1.2 × 0.75 = ?

solution.concept: Work left to right for × and ÷, then add; count decimal places carefully
solution.why_others_wrong: 1.4 takes 0.08 ÷ 0.016 as 0.5; 0.59 misplaces the decimal point in the final sum; 5.09 takes 1.2 × 0.75 as 0.09.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Which of the following arranges ∜6, ∛4, √2 and ⁶√10 in descending order?

solution.concept: Bring all the roots to a common index (the LCM of 4, 3, 2 and 6 is 12) and compare the 12th powers
solution.explanation: Raise each number to the 12th power: (∜6)¹² = 6³ = 216, (∛4)¹² = 4⁴ = 256, (√2)¹² = 2⁶ = 64 and (⁶√10)¹² = 10² = 100. So ∛4 > ∜6 > ⁶√10 > √2.
solution.why_others_wrong: ⁶√10 > ∜6 > ∛4 > √2 orders by the number under the root and ignores the index; √2 > ∛4 > ∜6 > ⁶√10 orders by the index alone; ∜6 > ∛4 > ⁶√10 > √2 swaps the top two, which would need 216 > 256.

solution.concept: Split each term: 1/(n(n + 1)(n + 2)) = ½ × [1/(n(n + 1)) − 1/((n + 1)(n + 2))], so the sum telescopes
solution.explanation: Each term is half the difference of two consecutive terms of 1/(n(n + 1)). Adding from n = 2 to n = 8, everything cancels except the first and the last: ½ × [1/(2 × 3) − 1/(9 × 10)] = ½ × (1/6 − 1/90) = ½ × 14/90 = 7/90.
solution.why_others_wrong: 7/45 forgets the factor ½; 1/12 keeps only the first part, ½ × 1/6; 11/144 ends the telescoping at 1/(8 × 9) instead of 1/(9 × 10).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What approximate value should come in place of the question mark (?)?
119.98% of 450.2 − 59.97% of 249.8 ≈ ?

solution.concept: Round each percentage and number; 120% of a number is the number plus one-fifth of it
solution.why_others_wrong: 690 adds the two parts instead of subtracting; 375 and 405 are 15 away from the exact value (about 390.3).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What approximate value should come in place of the question mark (?)?
√3249.2 + ∛2743.9 − 6.98 ≈ ?

solution.concept: Round to the nearest perfect square and cube: 3249 = 57², 2744 = 14³
solution.why_others_wrong: 71 ignores the − 6.98; 54 and 74 are 10 away from the exact value (about 64.0).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What approximate value should come in place of the question mark (?)?
(18.03 × 24.98) ÷ 14.97 + 9.02² ≈ ?

solution.concept: Round to whole numbers; cancel before multiplying
solution.why_others_wrong: 48 doubles 9 instead of squaring it (30 + 18); 121 and 101 are 10 away from the exact value (about 111.4).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What approximate value should come in place of the question mark (?)?
4.99³ − 3.01³ ≈ ?

solution.concept: Round the bases first, then cube each one separately
solution.why_others_wrong: 8 cubes the difference, (5 − 3)³; 152 adds the cubes; 16 squares instead of cubing (25 − 9).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What approximate value should come in place of the question mark (?)?
(√143.9 + √224.8)² ≈ ?

solution.concept: Find each square root first; the square of a sum is not the sum of the squares
solution.explanation: √143.9 ≈ 12 and √224.8 ≈ 15, so the bracket ≈ 27 and its square ≈ 729.
solution.why_others_wrong: 369 adds 144 and 225 and drops the cross term 2 × 12 × 15; 27 forgets to square; 784 = 28² takes √143.9 as 13.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What approximate value should come in place of the question mark (?)?
(65.02% of 1199.8) ÷ (12.98% of 299.7) ≈ ?

solution.concept: Round each percentage and number, evaluate both brackets, then divide
solution.why_others_wrong: 2 and 200 slip a decimal place; 26 takes 12.98% as 10% (780 ÷ 30).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What approximate value should come in place of the question mark (?)?
1/? of 3599.6 ≈ 14.98% of 1999.8

solution.concept: '1/? of N' means N ÷ ?; find the right side first

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What approximate value should come in place of the question mark (?)?
34.97% of (? − 120.3) ≈ 189.04

solution.concept: Divide by the percentage to find the bracket, then undo the subtraction
solution.why_others_wrong: 420 subtracts 120 instead of adding it; 540 is the value of the bracket, not of ?; 750 uses 30% instead of 35% (630 + 120).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What approximate value should come in place of the question mark (?)?
∜624.9 × ∛511.8 + 1/0.2498 ≈ ?

solution.concept: Use 625 = 5⁴ and 512 = 8³; the reciprocal of 0.25 is 4
solution.why_others_wrong: 40.25 adds 0.25 instead of its reciprocal; 204 takes the fourth root of 625 as its square root (25 × 8 + 4); 36 subtracts the 4.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What approximate value should come in place of the question mark (?)?
? × 3.01 ≈ √2304.2 × 6.01 + 40.02% of 819.6 − 16.98²

solution.concept: Round every term to a convenient value; finish the right side before dividing by the multiplier of ?
solution.why_others_wrong: 205 forgets to subtract 17²; 194 takes 17² as 34; 119 is 10 away from the exact value (about 109.0).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What approximate value should come in place of the question mark (?)?
(√? + 12.01) ÷ 2.998 ≈ 14.99% of 180.2

solution.concept: Work backwards: undo the division, then the addition, then the square root
solution.why_others_wrong: 6561 = 81² forgets to subtract 12; 69 is √?, not ?; 4225 = 65² is far from the exact value (about 4,757).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What approximate value should come in place of the question mark (?)?
?% of ? ≈ 144.02

solution.why_others_wrong: 12 solves ?² = 144 and forgets the ÷ 100; 1200 multiplies by 100 twice; 72 halves 144 as if ?% of ? were 2 × ?.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What approximate value should come in place of the question mark (?)?
12.02% of 24.98% of ? ≈ 31.96 ÷ 3.99 × 5.99

solution.concept: A percentage of a percentage is the product of the two decimals: 12% of 25% = 3%
solution.why_others_wrong: 160 slips a decimal place; 3200 takes 12% of 25% as 1.5%; 1920 takes 12.02% as 10% (48 ÷ 0.025).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What will come in place of the question mark (?) in the following series?
200, 164, 139, 123, 114, ?

solution.concept: The falls are the perfect squares 6², 5², 4², 3², … in decreasing order
solution.why_others_wrong: 113 subtracts 1², skipping 2²; 105 subtracts 9 again; 98 subtracts 16 (4²) again.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What will come in place of the question mark (?) in the following series?
13, 17, 25, 32, 37, 47, ?

solution.concept: Each term = previous term + the sum of its digits
solution.why_others_wrong: 57 adds 10 again; 59 adds 12; 52 adds 5, repeating an earlier jump. Only the digit-sum rule fits every step.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Find the missing number (?) in the series:
2, 6, 12, 20, ?, 42

solution.shortcut: The differences 4, 6, 8, 10, 12 rise by 2: 20 + 10 = 30.
solution.why_others_wrong: 28 adds 8 again; 32 adds 12, skipping 10; 36 = 6² does not lead to 42 by the rule.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Find the missing number (?) in the series:
96, 56, ?, 26, 21, 18.5

solution.why_others_wrong: 28 only halves 56 and forgets the + 8; 41 assumes equal steps from 56 to 26; 31 extends the last fall of 5 backwards to 26 + 5.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What will come in place of the question mark (?) in the following series?
8, 20, 50, 125, ?

solution.why_others_wrong: 250 multiplies by 2; 375 multiplies by 3; 437.5 multiplies by 3.5.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What will come in place of the question mark (?) in the following series?
6, 15, 33, 69, 141, ?

solution.shortcut: The differences 9, 18, 36, 72 double: next difference 144, and 141 + 144 = 285.
solution.why_others_wrong: 282 doubles and forgets the + 3; 288 adds 6 instead of 3; 213 adds 72 again.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What will come in place of the question mark (?) in the following series?
3, 10, 21, 36, 55, ?

solution.concept: Each term is n(2n + 1) = 2n² + n; the differences 7, 11, 15, 19 rise by 4
solution.why_others_wrong: 76 adds 21, raising the difference by 2 instead of 4; 74 adds 19 again; 81 = 9² does not fit n(2n + 1).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What will come in place of the question mark (?) in the following series?
5, 7, 12, 22, 39, 65, ?

solution.explanation: The differences are 2, 5, 10, 17, 26 = 1² + 1, 2² + 1, 3² + 1, 4² + 1, 5² + 1. The next is 6² + 1 = 37, so the term is 65 + 37 = 102.
solution.why_others_wrong: 101 adds 36 and forgets the + 1; 91 adds 26 again; 100 adds 35, repeating the last rise of 9 in the differences instead of 11.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What will come in place of the question mark (?) in the following series?
1, 2, 8, 48, 384, ?

solution.concept: The multipliers are the even numbers 2, 4, 6, 8, …
solution.why_others_wrong: 3,456 multiplies by 9; 4,608 multiplies by 12; 3,072 multiplies by 8 again.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What will come in place of the question mark (?) in the following series?
4, 6, 10, 17, 29, 48, ?

solution.concept: Take differences twice: the second differences are the prime numbers 2, 3, 5, 7, …
solution.explanation: First differences: 2, 4, 7, 12, 19. Second differences: 2, 3, 5, 7 — consecutive primes. The next second difference is 11, so the next first difference is 19 + 11 = 30 and the term is 48 + 30 = 78.
solution.why_others_wrong: 76 takes the second differences as odd numbers (next 9); 74 repeats the second difference 7; 80 skips 11 and uses 13.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What will come in place of the question mark (?) in the following series?
1, 9, 36, 100, 225, ?

solution.concept: Each term is the sum of the first n cubes, which equals the square of the n-th triangular number
solution.explanation: The differences are 8, 27, 64, 125 = 2³, 3³, 4³, 5³, so the next term is 225 + 6³ = 441. Equivalently the terms are 1², 3², 6², 10², 15², and the next triangular number is 21, giving 21² = 441.
solution.why_others_wrong: 361 = 19² continues the square roots 10, 15 by + 4; 450 doubles 225; 400 = 20² continues the roots by + 5 again.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Find the missing number (?) in the series:
1, 2, 5, 12, ?, 70, 169

solution.concept: Each term = 2 × previous term + the term before that
solution.why_others_wrong: 24 only doubles 12; 36 triples 12; 25 adds 1 to 2 × 12. None of them gives 70 at the next step (2 × 24 + 12 = 60, 2 × 36 + 12 = 84, 2 × 25 + 12 = 62).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Find the wrong number in the series:
100, 95, 85, 70, 50, 26, −5

solution.why_others_wrong: 85, 50 and −5 all fit the rule; −5 looks wrong only if 26 is taken as correct (26 − 30 = −4).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Find the wrong number in the series:
11, 33, 66, 110, 166, 231

solution.concept: The differences are 22, 33, 44, 55, 66: multiples of 11 (the terms are 11 × 1, 11 × 3, 11 × 6, …)
solution.shortcut: Every correct term is a multiple of 11; 166 is not.
solution.why_others_wrong: 66, 110 and 231 are 11 × 6, 11 × 10 and 11 × 21 and fit the pattern.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Find the wrong number in the series:
5, 40, 10, 34, 20, 28, 41, 22

solution.concept: Two series alternate: odd positions double (5, 10, 20, …) and even positions fall by 6 (40, 34, 28, …)
solution.explanation: Odd positions: 5, 10, 20, then 40 — but the series shows 41. Even positions: 40, 34, 28, 22 fall by 6 and fit. So 41 is wrong.
solution.why_others_wrong: 34, 20 and 22 belong to the two interleaved series and fit their rules.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Find the wrong number in the series:
2, 3, 5.5, 9.5, 15.5, 22, 30.5

solution.concept: The differences rise by 1.5 each time: 1, 2.5, 4, 5.5, 7, 8.5
solution.why_others_wrong: 5.5, 22 and 30.5 fit once 15.5 is corrected to 15; 22 looks off only if 15.5 is taken as correct.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Find the wrong number in the series:
3, 6, 18, 36, 106, 216, 648

solution.why_others_wrong: 18, 216 and 648 fit the alternating rule; 216 only looks wrong if 106 is taken as correct.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Find the wrong number in the series:
1, 3, 5, 11, 21, 42, 85

solution.concept: Each term = previous term + 2 × the term before it (equivalently × 2 + 1 and × 2 − 1 alternately)
solution.why_others_wrong: 11, 21 and 85 fit; 85 confirms 43, since 42 × 2 + 1 = 85 would need the rule to change.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Find the wrong number in the series:
1, 4, 8, 9, 26, 16, 64, 25

solution.concept: Two series alternate: odd positions are cubes (1³, 2³, 3³, 4³) and even positions are squares (2², 3², 4², 5²)
solution.explanation: Odd positions: 1, 8, ?, 64 = 1³, 2³, …, 4³, so the fifth term should be 3³ = 27, not 26. Even positions: 4, 9, 16, 25 = 2², 3², 4², 5² fit.
solution.why_others_wrong: 9, 16 and 64 are 3², 4² and 4³ and fit their series.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Both quadratics below have only negative roots. Find them and state how x compares with y.
I. x² + 13x + 42 = 0
II. y² + 17y + 72 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: When all coefficients are positive, both roots are negative; compare the smallest x with the largest y
solution.explanation: x = −6 or −7 and y = −8 or −9. The smallest x (−7) is greater than the largest y (−8), so x > y.
solution.why_others_wrong: x < y and x ≤ y come from dropping the minus signs (6 and 7 are smaller than 8 and 9).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Find the roots of the two equations and choose the relation between x and y, if any.
I. x² − 4x − 21 = 0
II. y² − 8y + 15 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: If one x lies above both y values and the other below them, no relation holds for every pair
solution.explanation: x = 7 or −3 and y = 3 or 5. x = 7 is greater than both y values but x = −3 is less than both, so the relationship cannot be established.
solution.why_others_wrong: x > y uses only x = 7; x ≤ y and x < y use only x = −3 (or read the root −3 as 3).
solution.final_answer: Option B: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Equation I has no x-term. Find all roots of I and II and pick the relation between x and y that holds for every pair.
I. 4x² − 25 = 0
II. 2y² + 13y + 21 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: x² = k gives two roots ±√k; do not drop the negative one
solution.explanation: I: x² = 25/4, so x = ±2.5. II: (2y + 7)(y + 3) = 0, so y = −3.5 or −3. Even the smaller x (−2.5) is greater than the larger y (−3), so x > y.
solution.why_others_wrong: x < y and x ≤ y come from reading the roots of II as +3 and +3.5.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Solve the two equations and mark the relation between x and y.
I. 3x² − 2x − 8 = 0
II. 3y² − 17y + 24 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Split the middle term; then compare the largest x with the smallest y
solution.explanation: I: (3x + 4)(x − 2) = 0, so x = 2 or −4/3. II: (3y − 8)(y − 3) = 0, so y = 8/3 or 3. The largest x (2) is below the smallest y (2.67), so x < y.
solution.why_others_wrong: x > y and x ≥ y come from a sign slip in II that gives y = −8/3 and −3.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
One equation is linear and the other quadratic. Solve both and choose the relation between x and y.
I. x/4 + x/6 = 5
II. y² − 21y + 108 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Solve the linear equation exactly; a common value makes the relation non-strict
solution.explanation: I: x/4 + x/6 = 5x/12 = 5, so x = 12. II: (y − 9)(y − 12) = 0, so y = 9 or 12. x = y when y = 12 and x > y when y = 9, so x ≥ y.
solution.why_others_wrong: x > y misses y = 12; x < y comes from forgetting to multiply the 5 by 12 when clearing the fractions (3x + 2x = 5 ⇒ x = 1).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Solve both equations (do not cancel a common factor that could be zero) and choose the relation between x and y.
I. x(x + 3) = 4(x + 3)
II. y² + 2y − 3 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Move everything to one side and factorise; dividing by (x + 3) would lose the root x = −3
solution.explanation: I: x(x + 3) − 4(x + 3) = (x + 3)(x − 4) = 0, so x = −3 or 4. II: (y + 3)(y − 1) = 0, so y = −3 or 1. x = 4 is greater than both y values, but x = −3 is less than y = 1. So the relationship cannot be established.
solution.why_others_wrong: x > y and x ≥ y come from cancelling (x + 3), which leaves only x = 4; x < y uses only x = −3.
solution.final_answer: Option D: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Solve both equations and choose the relation between x and y that holds for all their roots.
I. 12x² + 7x − 12 = 0
II. 20y² − 31y + 12 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Use the quadratic formula when splitting the middle term is slow; watch for a root common to both equations
solution.explanation: I: discriminant = 49 + 576 = 625, so x = (−7 ± 25)/24 = 3/4 or −4/3. II: discriminant = 961 − 960 = 1, so y = (31 ± 1)/40 = 4/5 or 3/4. x = y = 3/4 is possible and every other pair has x < y, so x ≤ y.
steps: All other pairs x < y ⇒ x ≤ y
solution.why_others_wrong: x < y misses the common root 3/4; x ≥ y holds only for the pair x = y = 3/4.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
The equations below have irrational coefficients (√2 ≈ 1.414). Solve them and choose the relation between x and y.
I. x² − 3√2x − 8 = 0
II. y² + 5√2y + 12 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Quadratic formula with surds: write the discriminant as a multiple of 2 so that its root is a multiple of √2
solution.explanation: I: discriminant = 18 + 32 = 50, √50 = 5√2, so x = (3√2 ± 5√2)/2 = 4√2 or −√2. II: discriminant = 50 − 48 = 2, so y = (−5√2 ± √2)/2 = −2√2 or −3√2. The smallest x (−√2 ≈ −1.41) is greater than the largest y (−2√2 ≈ −2.83), so x > y.
solution.why_others_wrong: x < y and x ≤ y come from taking the roots of II with the wrong sign (2√2 and 3√2).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Solve both equations without cancelling any factor that could be zero, and choose the relation between x and y.
I. (x − 4)² + 3(x − 4) = 0
II. 2y(y − 1) = y − 1

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Take the common bracket out as a factor; each factor can be zero
solution.explanation: I: (x − 4)[(x − 4) + 3] = (x − 4)(x − 1) = 0, so x = 4 or 1. II: 2y(y − 1) − (y − 1) = (y − 1)(2y − 1) = 0, so y = 1 or 1/2. x = 1, y = 1 gives x = y; every other pair has x > y. So x ≥ y.
steps: All other pairs x > y ⇒ x ≥ y
solution.why_others_wrong: x > y comes from cancelling (y − 1), which loses y = 1; x < y comes from writing the factors of I as (x + 4)(x + 1), which gives the negative roots −4 and −1.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Solve both equations (x ≠ 0) and choose the relation between x and y.
I. x/3 + 3/x = 10/3
II. y² − 25y + 156 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Clear the fractions by multiplying by 3x to get a quadratic
solution.explanation: I: multiply by 3x: x² + 9 = 10x, so x² − 10x + 9 = 0 and x = 1 or 9. II: (y − 12)(y − 13) = 0, so y = 12 or 13. The largest x (9) is below the smallest y (12), so x < y.
solution.why_others_wrong: x > y and x ≥ y come from a sign slip in II that gives y = −12 and −13; with the correct roots every x is below every y.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Solve both equations and choose the relation between x and y.
I. 9x² − 30x + 25 = 0
II. 3y² − 11y + 10 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: A perfect-square quadratic has one repeated root
solution.explanation: I: 9x² − 30x + 25 = (3x − 5)² = 0, so x = 5/3 only. II: (3y − 5)(y − 2) = 0, so y = 5/3 or 2. x = y when y = 5/3 and x < y when y = 2, so x ≤ y.
solution.why_others_wrong: x < y misses the common value 5/3; x > y comes from taking the roots of II as 5/3 and 2/3.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Which of the following numbers is divisible by both 4 and 9?

solution.concept: Divisible by 4: the last two digits form a multiple of 4. Divisible by 9: the digit sum is a multiple of 9
solution.explanation: 7,632: 32 is a multiple of 4 and 7 + 6 + 3 + 2 = 18 is a multiple of 9, so it is divisible by both (7,632 = 36 × 212).
steps: 5,418: digit sum 18 ✓ but 18 is not a multiple of 4
7,362: digit sum 18 ✓ but 62 is not a multiple of 4
solution.why_others_wrong: 5,418 and 7,362 pass the test for 9 but fail the test for 4 (7,362 has the same digits as 7,632 in another order); 8,724 passes the test for 4 but its digit sum, 21, is only a multiple of 3.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A hall floor measuring 9.6 m by 7.2 m is to be paved with identical square tiles, with no tile cut. What is the least number of tiles needed?

solution.concept: The largest square tile that fits exactly has a side equal to the HCF of the two lengths
solution.explanation: In cm the floor is 960 × 720. HCF(960, 720) = 240, so the largest tile is 240 cm × 240 cm. Tiles needed = (960 ÷ 240) × (720 ÷ 240) = 4 × 3 = 12.
solution.why_others_wrong: 48 uses 120 cm tiles, a common factor but not the highest; 108 uses 80 cm tiles; 240 is the side of the tile in cm, not the number of tiles.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What is the remainder when 17²³ + 23²³ is divided by 40?

solution.concept: For an odd power n, aⁿ + bⁿ is always divisible by a + b
solution.explanation: 23 is odd, so 17²³ + 23²³ is divisible by 17 + 23 = 40. The remainder is 0.
steps: aⁿ + bⁿ is divisible by a + b when n is odd
solution.shortcut: Check: 17²³ leaves 33 and 23²³ leaves 7 on division by 40; 33 + 7 = 40.
solution.why_others_wrong: 33 is the remainder of 17²³ alone; 7 is the remainder of 23²³ alone; 2 treats both powers as leaving remainder 1, a rule that holds only for suitable even powers.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: How many factors of 2⁴ × 3³ × 5² are perfect squares?

solution.concept: A factor is a perfect square when every prime in it has an even power
solution.explanation: A square factor is 2ᵃ × 3ᵇ × 5ᶜ with a, b and c even: a ∈ {0, 2, 4} (3 ways), b ∈ {0, 2} (2 ways), c ∈ {0, 2} (2 ways). So there are 3 × 2 × 2 = 12 such factors.
solution.why_others_wrong: 60 counts all factors, (4 + 1)(3 + 1)(2 + 1); 4 counts the perfect-cube factors; 30 assumes half of all factors are squares.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What is the largest number that divides 1,305, 4,665 and 6,905 and leaves the same remainder in each case?

solution.concept: If three numbers leave the same remainder on division by d, then d divides every difference; take the HCF of the differences
solution.why_others_wrong: 560 also leaves equal remainders but is not the largest such number; 2,240 is one of the differences but does not divide 3,360; 185 is the common remainder, not the divisor.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: If 30% of A equals 45% of B, then B is what percentage of A?

solution.concept: Equal parts of A and B: 0.30A = 0.45B, so B/A = 30/45
solution.why_others_wrong: 150% is A as a percentage of B; 33⅓% is how much less B is than A; 15% is the difference between the two percentages.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A laptop bought for ₹60,000 loses 15% of its value in the first year and, in the second year, 10% of its value at the start of that year. What is its value after 2 years?

solution.why_others_wrong: ₹45,000 subtracts 25% of the original price at once; ₹51,000 stops after the first year; ₹43,350 applies 15% in both years.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: For positive numbers x, y and z, x% of y is 75 and y% of z is 120. What percentage of x is z?

solution.concept: Write both statements as products: xy/100 = 75 and yz/100 = 120; divide to cancel y
solution.explanation: x% of y = xy/100 = 75 and y% of z = yz/100 = 120. Dividing, z/x = 120/75 = 1.6, so z is 160% of x.
solution.why_others_wrong: 62.5% is x as a percentage of z; 45% reads the difference 120 − 75 as a percentage; 60% is how much more z is than x, written as if it were the whole.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The value of a machine fell from ₹2,50,000 to ₹1,60,000 in 2 years. If it depreciated at the same rate each year (on its value at the start of that year), what was the annual rate of depreciation?

solution.concept: Value after n years = original × (1 − r)ⁿ; take the n-th root of the ratio
solution.why_others_wrong: 18% treats the fall as simple (36% ÷ 2); 36% is the total fall over 2 years; 40% takes the square root of 0.36 (the fall) instead of 0.64 (what remains).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Ravi saves 25% of his income. His income rises by 20%, and he now saves 20% of the new income. By what percentage does his expenditure rise?

solution.concept: Take the old income as 100 and work out both expenditures
solution.explanation: Old: income 100, savings 25, expenditure 75. New: income 120, savings 20% of 120 = 24, expenditure 96. Expenditure rises by 21 on 75, i.e. 28%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 20% assumes expenditure rises with income; 4% is the fall in savings (25 → 24); 21% reads the rise of 21 on an income of 100 as a percentage of expenditure.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A 20% fall in the price of sugar lets a household buy 5 kg more sugar for ₹600. What was the original price per kg?

solution.concept: The money saved on the old quantity buys the extra quantity at the new price
solution.explanation: A 20% fall saves 20% of ₹600 = ₹120, and this buys the extra 5 kg, so the new price is 120 ÷ 5 = ₹24 per kg. The original price was 24 ÷ 0.8 = ₹30 per kg.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹24 is the new price; ₹28.80 adds 20% to ₹24 instead of dividing by 0.8; ₹60 reads the 20% fall as a ₹20 fall per kg.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Two numbers are in the ratio 5 : 8 and their difference is 45. What is their sum?

solution.explanation: 3 parts = 45, so 1 part = 15. The numbers are 75 and 120, and their sum is 13 parts = 195.
solution.why_others_wrong: 120 is the larger number; 75 is the smaller number; 585 multiplies 45 by 13 without first dividing by 3.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: If (x + 3) : (x + 11) = (x − 2) : (x + 2), what is the value of x?

solution.concept: In a proportion a : b = c : d, the product of the extremes equals the product of the means: ad = bc
solution.why_others_wrong: −7/3 multiplies the wrong pairs, (x + 3)(x − 2) = (x + 11)(x + 2); 5.5 drops the constant 6 when expanding; 28 stops at 4x = 28.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The incomes of A, B and C are in the ratio 7 : 9 : 12 and their expenditures are in the ratio 8 : 9 : 15. If A saves one-fourth of his income, what is the ratio of the savings of A, B and C?

solution.concept: Use one unit for incomes and another for expenditures; A's saving links the two units
solution.explanation: Let the incomes be 7k, 9k and 12k. A saves 7k/4, so A spends 21k/4 = 8 parts of expenditure, and one expenditure part = 21k/32. Then B spends 189k/32 and saves 288k/32 − 189k/32 = 99k/32; C spends 315k/32 and saves 384k/32 − 315k/32 = 69k/32; A saves 56k/32. Ratio 56 : 99 : 69.
solution.why_others_wrong: 7 : 9 : 12 assumes everyone saves a quarter; 8 : 9 : 15 is the expenditure ratio; 69 : 99 : 56 lists the savings in reverse order.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The price of a diamond varies directly as the square of its weight. A diamond worth ₹1,44,000 breaks into three pieces whose weights are in the ratio 1 : 2 : 3. What is the loss caused by the breakage?

solution.concept: Price ∝ weight², so compare the sum of the squares of the parts with the square of the whole
solution.explanation: Whole weight = 6 parts, so its price corresponds to 6² = 36 units: 1 unit = ₹4,000. The pieces are worth 1², 2² and 3² units = 14 units = ₹56,000. Loss = 1,44,000 − 56,000 = ₹88,000.
